title: The Apacheans to the Southwest, c. AD 1000–1500
summary: The Apache and Navajo speak Southern Athabaskan languages, whose relatives lie far to the north in Canada and Alaska. Their ancestors came south, probably along the Plains or the Rockies, and reached the Southwest by about 1500. The date and the road are among the oldest arguments in the region's archaeology.

legs.source: Apache (Wikipedia) and Navajo (Wikipedia): a migration from the north, the date and route argued
legs.doubt: Whether they came down the Plains, the Rockies or the Great Basin, and whether before 1300 or only about 1500, is argued; the line is one of the proposed ways.

events.label: The northern homeland
events.text: The Athabaskan languages have most of their speakers in the north-west interior of Canada and in Alaska, which is why their homeland is looked for there.

events.label: Dinétah and the Southwest
events.text: The Navajo homeland, Dinétah, lies in north-west New Mexico. In April 1541 Coronado's men met people on the plains they called Querechos, possibly Plains Apache. The Navajo took over much of the pueblo way of life.
